newsitem.title: USA: Parts of missing A-10 found on Colorado mountain.
newsitem.headline: Parts of missing A-10 found on Colorado mountain.

text.p: Small metal parts recovered from wreckage on a snowy peak in the Rocky Mountains on Wednesday came from a warplane that disappeared three weeks ago carrying four bombs, the Air Force said.
The identification of the aircraft parts confirmed what the Air Force had earlier assumed -- that the A-10 Thurderbolt crashed into the side of the mountain.

But helicopter crewmen who reached the site earlier on Wednesday found no trace in the snow-buried wreckage of the pilot or the bombs the plane was carrying. The A-10 disappeared during a routine training mission on April 2.
"I can tell you ... we have positively identified that these are pieces of the A-10 aircraft," Air Force Maj.-Gen. Nels Running told reporters.
"I don't know if Capt. (Craig) Button was with the aircraft or not with the aircraft, so I can't talk about remains. The search continues," he said.
The weather forecast for Thursday was not encouraging for further flights to the crash site, Running said.

At an earlier briefing, Running said a crewman from an MH-53 heavy-lift helicopter was lowered to the side of the mountain where wreckage was spotted. However, the largest piece of wreckage visible through snow was too big to lift.

The crewman retrieved a cable assembly and a piece believed to be from a military-type plane engine. Two A-10 pilots were at the rescue headquarters in Eagle, Colorado, to examine the pieces of wreckage and later identified them as coming from Button's plane.
The A-10 Thunderbolt attack bomber is thought to have slammed into the side of the 12,500-foot (3,800-metre) -high New York Mountain in the remote Sawatch range southeast of the Vail ski resort.
The wreckage was spotted on Sunday by an Army National Guard helicopter crew near a steep cliff on New York Mountain.

Air Force officials have been at a loss to explain why Button, 32, left the three-plane delta formation in which he was flying and apparently veered northeast into Colorado, some 850 miles (1,350 km) away from a training exercise.

Button, whose plane was carrying four 500-pound (225-kg) Mark 82 conventional bombs, broke formation after leaving the Davis-Monthan Air Force Base near Tucson, Arizona, en route for the Barry M. Goldwater Bombing Range in Arizona.
